name: Fairgate Roads Authority — heavy vehicle access permits
brief: Fairgate issues about 12,000 heavy vehicle access permits a year. An operator applies for a route, an assessor checks it against mass and bridge limits, affected road managers consent, and a permit is issued. It currently takes about 40 days. A new national scheme obliges Fairgate to decide routine applications within 15 days from 1 July, and the authority has no idea whether that is achievable.
closing: Sixteen techniques, each taking something the one before it produced. Nothing here is a fresh start: the process model becomes the analysis rows, the worst row becomes the root cause, the cost to serve becomes the business case, the scope becomes the functions, the functions become the rules and the use cases, and the benefit becomes the KPI. That chain is what makes a technique useful — on its own each is a drawing, in sequence they are an argument.

steps.question: Who is affected, and who actually decides?
steps.takes: Nothing — this is the first pass.
steps.gives: Eight parties positioned by influence and interest. Road managers turn out to hold a veto nobody had planned around.

artefact.title: Who matters, and how much
artefact.note: Road managers are external to Fairgate and consent individually. That is the first sign the 15-day obligation is not entirely within Fairgate's control.

steps.question: What do the existing artefacts already answer?
steps.takes: The stakeholder list, which says who owns which document.
steps.gives: What is already settled, and the three questions only a person can answer. Those become the interview guide.

artefact.title: Read before anyone's time is booked
rows: Why 2 of them are skipped at volume
Whether that runs concurrently or in series
Whether route data is reliable enough to automate
artefact.note: The consent question matters most: 11 councils at 10 days in series cannot fit inside 15 days at all.

steps.question: What do assessors actually do, as opposed to what the procedure says?
steps.takes: The two unexplained checks from the document analysis.
steps.gives: The real practice, including a shortcut nobody had documented. Feeds the current-state process model.

artefact.title: Six documented checks, watched across nine applications
rows: 'Known' is the assessor's memory, not a register
Restriction data sits in a separate system nobody opens
artefact.note: Two of the six checks rely on recall rather than data. Both are the checks that generate rework when a road manager objects.

steps.question: What is the end-to-end flow, and where does it change hands?
steps.takes: The observed practice, not the documented procedure.
steps.gives: Four stages and the hand-offs between them. These four stage names are used unchanged by every later step.

artefact.title: Current state — application to permit

flows.label: objection — reassess, and the clock restarts

artefact.note: Consent sits in a lane Fairgate does not own. Every objection returns the file to assessment and restarts the elapsed clock.

steps.question: Where do the 40 days actually go?
steps.takes: The four stages from the process model, by the same names.
steps.gives: Elapsed against touch time, and a cost to serve of $41 a permit. Both are consumed by the business case.

artefact.title: 40 days elapsed, 3.2 hours of work
artefact.note: Cost to serve is $41 a permit across 12,000 permits, so $492,000 a year. Adding assessors buys touch time, which is 1.1% of the problem.

steps.question: Why does route assessment take 19 days to do 2.1 hours of work?
steps.takes: The worst row of the process analysis.
steps.gives: A cause that is about data, not effort. That rules out the obvious option before it is costed.

artefact.title: Why route assessment runs to 19 days

nodes.label: Route assessment takes 19 days for 2.1 hours of work

children.label: Why? Files wait to be reworked after objections
Why? Road managers object to routes already assessed
Bridge and seasonal restriction data is not on the assessor's screen
Why? Assessors batch work to avoid switching systems
Why? Restriction data lives in a second system
The same root: the data an assessment needs is not where the assessment happens

artefact.note: Both branches end in the same place, which is what makes it a root cause rather than two problems.

steps.question: What is each option worth?
steps.takes: The $41 cost to serve, and the root cause that says more assessors will not help.
steps.gives: Three options valued over five years at 7%. B has the best NPV, C the fastest payback.

artefact.title: Three options, five years, discounted at 7%
artefact.note: Option A is the one the executive asked for. It adds touch-time capacity to a queue problem and returns a negative NPV, which is exactly what the root cause predicted.

steps.question: B has the better return and C pays back sooner. Which?
steps.takes: The NPV and payback figures, unchanged.
steps.gives: A recommendation with the weighting visible, so the argument is about criteria rather than preference.

artefact.title: Weighted against criteria agreed before scoring
artefact.note: C pays back faster and still loses, because payback carries 15% of the decision and the statutory obligation carries 40%. Naming the weights first is what stops that being an argument about opinions.

steps.question: What could stop option B working?
steps.takes: The recommended option, and the road manager veto from the stakeholder map.
steps.gives: An expected monetary value of $196,000, which goes into the business case beside the benefit.

artefact.title: Option B risks, post-mitigation
artefact.note: Expected monetary value across all outcomes is $196,000. That figure enters the business case; the severe cases stay here.

steps.question: Is the change justified, and on what?
steps.takes: Need, options, value, risk — each already produced by a step above.
steps.gives: An approved change strategy. Nothing new is invented here; the case is an assembly.

panels.label: Need
items: 40 days today, 1.1% of it working time

panels.label: Options considered
items: C outsource — faster payback, loses capability
B rules engine and self-service — recommended

panels.label: Timing
items: Consent redesign is on the critical path

steps.question: What is in, what is out, and what will try to creep in?
steps.gives: A boundary. The in-scope list becomes the top level of the decomposition, unchanged.

artefact.title: Boundary for the permit service change
artefact.note: Restriction data is adjacent and unavoidable: the root cause sits in it. Naming it here forces the decision rather than absorbing it silently.

steps.question: What does the in-scope work break into?
steps.takes: The four in-scope items, as the top level.
steps.gives: Functions small enough to specify. 'Assess route' is where the rules and the data live.

artefact.title: The permit service, broken down far enough to specify

nodes.label: Issue a heavy vehicle access permit

steps.question: What governs an assessment, and how often will it change?
steps.gives: Rules held apart from the process. Each names the data elements it needs, which sets the dictionary.

artefact.title: Assessment rules, governed separately from the workflow
rows: A route crossing a bridge below the vehicle's gross mass is refused.
A route under a seasonal restriction is refused for the restricted dates.
An application matching a refusal within 12 months goes to panel.
Consent is required from every road manager on the route.
artefact.note: The scheme rules changed twice last year. Held in workflow code each change is a release; held here each change is a rule version.

steps.question: What exactly are the elements those rules depend on?
steps.takes: The data column of the rules table.
steps.gives: Element definitions precise enough to build and to migrate.

artefact.title: Elements the assessment rules depend on
rows: Total mass of vehicle and load
Rated capacity of a structure on the route
First day a seasonal restriction applies
The council or authority controlling a road segment
Date of the most recent refusal for this operator and route
artefact.note: restriction_from and restriction_to are the elements the observed shortcut skipped. Defining them is what moves the check from memory to data.

steps.question: What may a permit become, and from where?
steps.takes: The process stages and the refusal rule.
steps.gives: Permitted transitions, including two that must be forbidden.

artefact.title: Permit lifecycle
artefact.note: The objection loop back to Assessed is the one the process model showed restarting the clock. It is legal, and it is the thing the 15-day obligation cannot absorb twice.

steps.question: How will anyone know whether it worked?
steps.takes: The benefits claimed in the business case, and the states just defined.
steps.gives: Measures with targets and the threshold at which someone must act. This is what closes the loop back to step 5.

artefact.title: From the obligation down to the indicator someone acts on

nodes.label: Decide routine permits within 15 days at $19 a permit

children.label: Put restriction and bridge data on the assessment screen
Median days Lodged to Issued — target ≤ 15, act above 13
Seek consent from all road managers at once
Median consent days — target ≤ 7, act above 9
Councils consenting digitally — target ≥ 9 of 11, act below 7

artefact.note: Baseline is step 5: 40 days, $41 a permit. Without that row there is no improvement to claim, only an assertion.
